common_name: Brazilian Red Hots Alternanthera (Hot Pink and Rose Calico Plant)

planting.note: Set out transplants once soil has warmed well past the last frost; foliage color saturates fastest in a spot getting strong morning or all-day sun.

directions: Brazilian Red Hots is a Texas Superstar-designated selection of Alternanthera dentata grown purely for its glowing rose-pink and hot-coral foliage rather than its insignificant flowers. It forms a tidy, mounded clump that holds its shape without much pruning, making it a dependable filler for mixed borders, mass edging, or container combinations. Color intensifies with more direct sun exposure, while light afternoon shade in the hottest part of summer keeps the leaves from looking stressed in zone 9's peak heat. Pinch any reverted all-green shoots promptly, since they will otherwise outgrow and dilute the colorful variegation.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

planting.note: Plant after the soil has warmed in full sun for the brightest leaf color; morning sun with afternoon shade is an acceptable second choice.

directions: A 2004 Georgia Gold Medal winner, Chartreuse Alternanthera forms a low, dense, compact mound of glowing yellow-green foliage that holds its color from spring through fall frost without fading in summer heat. It is tough and low-maintenance, tolerating heat and humidity far better than many bright-foliage annuals, and works well as a continuous color band along a bed edge or as a high-contrast companion to purple or burgundy foliage plants. Shear lightly if growth becomes loose or leggy to renew density and leaf color. Grown entirely for foliage, its small flowers are insignificant and not worth preserving.
sources: Georgia Gold Medal Plant Program (Georgia Plant Selections Committee / University of Georgia)
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — CAES Field Report

common_name: Athens Gem Plectranthus (Mottled Chartreuse Foliage Spurflower)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or transplants after frost danger passes into humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright but filtered light; strong all-day sun can bleach the delicate leaf mottling.

directions: Introduced through the University of Georgia's ornamental plant program and a Georgia Gold Medal winner, Athens Gem is grown for its soft, irregularly mottled foliage shifting through shades of apple-green, olive, and chartreuse. It thrives in part shade to bright filtered light, where the subtle color variation reads best, since harsh full sun tends to wash out the mottling and can scorch the relatively soft leaves. Use it as a filler in shaded containers, hanging baskets, or mixed borders where its loose, trailing habit softens edges. Pinch growing tips periodically to keep the plant full and to delay the inconspicuous flower spikes, which are not ornamentally important.
sources: Georgia Gold Medal Plant Program (Georgia Plant Selections Committee / University of Georgia)
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — CAES Field Report

common_name: Nova Pentas (Vigorous Rose-Pink Egyptian Star Cluster)

planting.note: Transplant into full sun once the soil is warm and frost danger has passed; Nova grows noticeably larger than compact bedding pentas, so give it extra room.

directions: A 1999 Georgia Gold Medal winner, Nova is one of the largest and most vigorous pentas cultivars, growing into a substantial, upright sub-shrub topped from late spring through fall frost with wide, 3-to-4-inch clusters of star-shaped rose-pink flowers that draw butterflies and hummingbirds reliably. Its bigger scale compared to compact bedding pentas suits it to the back of a mixed border or as a standalone flowering mass rather than tight edging. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continued rebloom, and established plants tolerate Gulf Coast heat and humidity with minimal disease trouble given full sun and decent drainage.
sources: Georgia Gold Medal Plant Program (Georgia Plant Selections Committee / University of Georgia)
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — CAES Field Report

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Athena tolerates compacted urban soils and heat well once established.

directions: Cloned from a venerable lacebark elm on the University of Georgia's Athens campus and released by Dr. Michael Dirr's breeding program, Athena was a 1995 Georgia Gold Medal winner recognized for its uniform, broadly rounded crown and dense, tidy habit compared to seed-grown lacebark elms. Its exfoliating bark, mottled in tan, gray, and orange-brown patches, adds winter and summer interest as a specimen or street tree. It tolerates heat, drought, and the compacted, poor soils common in urban plantings far better than American elm, while showing good resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle. Give it full sun and room to reach its mature rounded spread, and expect minimal pruning needs beyond removing occasional crossing branches while young.
sources: Georgia Gold Medal Plant Program (Georgia Plant Selections Committee / University of Georgia)
Dr. Michael A. Dirr — University of Georgia ornamental plant breeding records
